PHSCS 587

Minority-carrier diffusion

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows why an injected minority population decays away from a junction

A forward-biased junction injects minority carriers into the adjacent quasi-neutral material. Let u measure distance away from the injecting edge into a p-type region, and let Δn(u) = n(u) − np0 be excess minority-electron concentration. With negligible electric field, uniform Dn and low-injection lifetime τn, steady continuity becomes Dn d²Δn/du² − Δn/τn = 0.

For a semi-infinite region with Δn(0) fixed by injection and Δn → 0 far away, the solution is Δn(u) = Δn(0)exp(−u/Ln), where Ln = √(Dnτn). Ln has units of length and is the distance over which the excess concentration falls by a factor e in this particular geometry. It compares the time available before recombination with the rate of diffusive spreading.

An actual contact at finite distance, a recombining surface, a nonuniform field or high injection changes the boundary-value problem. The exponential profile should therefore be tied to its assumptions. Electron particle flux travels down this profile; its conventional diffusion current has the opposite direction. A junction’s terminal current includes the corresponding hole contribution as well.

Example

If lifetime increases by a factor of nine while Dn stays fixed, Ln increases by a factor of three. The profile extends farther from the injecting edge before reaching the same normalized concentration.

Practice

1. What happens to the normalized concentration at u = Ln?

Substitute into the exponential.

It is e⁻¹, approximately 0.368 of its edge value.

2. Why can a nearby extracting contact change the exponential profile?

Reconsider the far-boundary condition.

The semi-infinite solution requires the excess to vanish only far away. A finite contact imposes a different condition at a finite distance, so the full solution must satisfy that condition.
